jd.m1.1.q: x has shape [7, 4096] and W has shape [4096, 1024]. What shape does x @ W get?
jd.m1.1.e: The last axis of x (4096) must match the first axis of W. It is replaced by W’s second axis: [7, 1024]. The 7 rows are processed independently.
jd.m1.2.q: Two nonzero vectors have dot product 0. What does that mean?
jd.m1.2.e: a·b = |a||b|cos θ. Since both lengths are nonzero, cos θ = 0: the vectors are orthogonal (90°). The projection of either onto the other is zero. This is a geometric statement, not statistical independence.
jd.m1.2.o1: They are parallel, pointing in the same direction
jd.m1.2.o2: They are orthogonal, with no component along each other
jd.m1.2.o3: They are parallel, pointing in opposite directions
jd.m1.2.o4: They have equal lengths, regardless of their directions
jd.m1.3.q: Three compatible linear layers are stacked with no activation function between them. What kind of mapping do they express?
jd.m1.3.e: x @ W1 @ W2 @ W3 = x @ (W1 W2 W3). The product is still one matrix: stacking alone introduces no non-linearity.
jd.m1.3.o1: A nonlinear map that cannot reduce to one matrix
jd.m1.3.o2: A linear map equivalent to a single matrix
jd.m1.3.o3: A constant map independent of the input values
jd.m1.3.o4: A map restricted to nonnegative output values
jd.m1.4.q: You add 10 to every logit before softmax. What happens to the probabilities?
jd.m1.4.e: Softmax depends only on the differences between logits. A constant in all of them cancels out.
jd.m1.4.o1: Every token probability increases by the same amount
jd.m1.4.o2: The highest-probability token takes all the probability
jd.m1.4.o3: The probability distribution stays exactly the same
jd.m1.4.o4: The probability distribution moves closer to uniform
jd.m1.5.q: In a dense layer, a token vector is multiplied by a learned matrix. Which weights participate?
jd.m1.5.e: Dense matrix multiplication uses all entries, even if some inputs are zero. The weights stay fixed during inference; the computed activations depend on the token.
jd.m1.5.o3: All entries of the weight matrix
jd.m1.5.o4: Only the row selected by the token id
jd.m2.1.q: What decides how a text is split into tokens?
jd.m2.1.e: For a fixed tokenizer and settings, the same text produces the same token ids. In BPE, the vocabulary and merge rules are fixed before model training.
jd.m2.1.o1: The model’s learned weights during each forward pass
jd.m2.1.o2: The fixed vocabulary and rules of the tokenizer
jd.m2.1.o3: The role labels chosen by the chat template
jd.m2.1.o4: The probability cutoff chosen by the sampler
jd.m2.2.q: What does a chat template do?
jd.m2.2.e: The model only sees one long token sequence. The template inserts special tokens that mark where each role starts and ends.
jd.m2.2.o1: Summarizes messages to fit the context window
jd.m2.2.o2: Chooses a system instruction for the topic
jd.m2.2.o3: Serializes messages with role and turn markers
jd.m2.3.q: Why is embedding called a lookup rather than a matrix multiplication?
jd.m2.3.e: x = E[ids]. No arithmetic, just copying rows. The table is learned, though, just like every other weight.
jd.m2.3.o1: Each id is multiplied by every row in the table
jd.m2.3.o2: Each id selects one learned row from the table
jd.m2.3.o3: Each id is used to compute a new row at runtime
jd.m2.3.o4: Each id selects one column instead of one row
jd.m2.4.q: With the course’s subword tokenizer, how does the token count of ordinary Swedish text typically compare with its word count?
jd.m2.4.e: Many Swedish words split into several tokens, and punctuation also contributes. There is no fixed tokens-per-word ratio: count with the model’s tokenizer for an exact result.
jd.m3.1.e: The original had an encoder and a decoder. Decoder-only models like GPT and Llama have just one stack with a causal mask.
jd.m3.1.o1: An encoder stack where every position sees the whole input
jd.m3.1.o2: A causal generating stack without a separate encoder
jd.m3.1.o3: A decoder stack that reads a separate encoder’s output
jd.m3.1.o4: A generating stack where attention is replaced by an MLP
jd.m3.2.q: Why does the stream have the same shape [T, 4096] after every block?
jd.m3.2.e: The output of one block must fit as the input of the next, and x + contribution requires the same shape.
jd.m3.2.o1: To reuse the same weights in every block without retraining
jd.m3.2.o2: To stack blocks and add contributions with matching shapes
jd.m3.2.o3: To give every position its own vocabulary-sized vector
jd.m3.2.o4: To keep attention from reading information at other positions
jd.m3.3.q: Why is a final RMSNorm needed before the LM head in Llama?
jd.m3.3.e: Blocks add to the stream without normalizing it; they normalize copies they read. A final normalization sets its scale before the LM head.
jd.m3.3.o1: To change the stream width to the vocabulary size
jd.m3.3.o2: To rescale the stream after its unnormalized additions
jd.m3.3.o3: To average the token vectors into a single shared vector
jd.m3.3.o4: To replace the learned matrix used by the LM head
jd.m3.4.q: How many weight matrices are there in one layer of Llama-3-8B (not counting the norm vectors)?
jd.m3.4.e: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo in attention, W_gate, W_up and W_down in the MLP. On top of that, two norm vectors of 4096.
jd.m3.5.q: What happens to x in the line x = x + Attention(RMSNorm(x))?
jd.m3.5.e: RMSNorm is applied to a copy. The stream itself changes only through the addition.
jd.m3.5.o1: Normalize x, then replace it with the attention output
jd.m3.5.o2: Add attention of a normalized copy to the original x
jd.m3.5.o3: Add attention of x, then normalize the resulting sum
jd.m3.5.o4: Add attention of x to a normalized copy of x
jd.m3.6.q: Which statement about the MLP is correct?
jd.m3.6.e: The MLP works within each token’s vector. Information between positions is exchanged by attention, not by the MLP.
jd.m3.6.o2: Tokens are processed separately, with shared weights
jd.m3.6.o3: Tokens are processed separately, with position-specific weights
jd.m3.7.q: Where in the block do tokens exchange information with each other?
jd.m3.7.e: The MLP, the normalization and the addition work on each position separately. Attention is the only place where one position reads from others.
jd.m3.7.o1: In the MLP’s expansion and projection
jd.m3.7.o2: In the normalization of each token vector
jd.m3.7.o3: In attention’s weighted mix of values
jd.m3.7.o4: In the addition to each token’s residual stream
jd.m3.8.q: What shape does K have in one layer of Llama-3-8B for T tokens, after splitting into heads?
jd.m3.8.e: 8 KV heads of 128 dimensions each. Q has 32 heads; four query heads share each KV head (GQA).
jd.m3.9.q: What does the causal mask guarantee?
jd.m3.9.e: Scores against later positions are set to −∞ and become 0 after softmax. So nothing changes for an old position when new tokens arrive.
jd.m3.9.o1: A position can read only itself and earlier positions
jd.m3.9.o2: A position can read any position except itself
jd.m3.9.o3: Each head must read a different set of token positions
jd.m3.9.o4: A position can read only the preceding block of tokens
jd.m3.10.q: How does a layer update the residual stream?
jd.m3.10.e: x = x + contribution. The shape [T, 4096] is the same through all layers.
jd.m3.10.o1: It replaces the stream with the contribution
jd.m3.10.o2: It multiplies the stream by the contribution
jd.m3.10.o3: It adds the contribution to the stream
jd.m3.10.o4: It concatenates the stream and the contribution
jd.m3.11.e: The rotation happens inside each attention layer, on Q and K. V and the residual stream are not touched.
jd.m3.11.o1: Adds a position-dependent vector to the embeddings
jd.m3.11.o2: Rotates Q and K according to their token positions
jd.m3.11.o3: Rotates V to encode position in the cached values
jd.m3.11.o4: Removes scores for positions later in the sequence
jd.m4.1.q: How many numbers do the logits contain for one position in Llama-3-8B?
jd.m4.1.e: One number per token in the vocabulary.
jd.m4.2.q: What does temperature 0.5 do compared with 1.0?
jd.m4.2.e: The logits are divided by the temperature. Less than 1 amplifies the differences.
jd.m4.2.o1: Keeps a fixed half of the most likely candidates
jd.m4.2.o2: Sharpens probabilities toward the highest logits
jd.m4.2.o3: Flattens probabilities toward a uniform distribution
jd.m4.2.o4: Keeps only candidates above a fixed probability cutoff
jd.m4.3.e: The number of candidates adapts: few when the model is confident, many when it is unsure.
jd.m4.3.o1: All tokens with individual probability at least 0.9
jd.m4.3.o2: The highest-ranked 90% of the vocabulary by token count
jd.m4.3.o3: The smallest top-ranked set reaching total probability 0.9
jd.m4.3.o4: All tokens whose probabilities are within 0.9 of the largest
jd.m4.4.q: Why does ordinary autoregressive generation choose output tokens sequentially?
jd.m4.4.e: During training the whole text is known and everything is computed in one pass. During generation the next token does not exist until it has been drawn.
jd.m4.4.o1: The GPU must reload the model before every new token
jd.m4.4.o2: Each next prediction needs the previously chosen token
jd.m4.4.o3: Attention cannot process several known positions together
jd.m4.4.o4: The tokenizer must finish decoding before the next forward pass
jd.m5.1.q: What is the target for position t during pretraining?
jd.m5.1.e: The targets are the inputs shifted one step.
jd.m5.1.o1: The input token at position t
jd.m5.1.o2: The next token, at position t + 1
jd.m5.1.o3: The preceding token, at position t − 1
jd.m5.1.o4: The final token of the entire sequence
jd.m5.2.q: Why can training compute the loss for all positions in a single forward pass?
jd.m5.2.e: This is called teacher forcing. The mask means position t only sees 0..t even though everything sits in the same tensor.
jd.m5.2.o1: The optimizer predicts targets before the forward pass
jd.m5.2.o2: Known targets and a causal mask allow parallel predictions
jd.m5.2.o3: Removing the causal mask lets each position read its target
jd.m5.2.o4: A KV cache contains all predictions from the preceding batch
jd.m5.3.q: In an illustrative mixed-precision AdamW setup with 16-bit weights and gradients, fp32 master weights and two fp32 optimizer states, roughly how much memory is used per parameter, excluding activations?
jd.m5.3.e: 2 bytes for the weight + 2 for the gradient + 4 for the master weight + 8 for the two Adam states = 16 bytes. Activations add more. Other precision and optimizer configurations have different totals.
jd.m5.4.q: What does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) usually do when turning a base model into a chat assistant?
jd.m5.4.e: SFT trains on example dialogues, typically applying next-token loss to assistant responses. The transformer architecture can stay the same; the updated weights learn the response format and behavior.
jd.m5.4.o2: It adds an attention stack for each role
jd.m5.4.o3: It learns assistant behavior from example responses
jd.m5.4.o4: It replaces tokens with a fixed list of replies
jd.m6.1.q: For a large dense model resident on the GPU, what usually limits single-sequence decode at short context?
jd.m6.1.e: Each step streams the dense weights to compute just one new token. At short context this is typically memory-bandwidth-bound, not limited by peak arithmetic throughput.
jd.m6.1.o1: The rate of arithmetic on the GPU’s compute units
jd.m6.1.o2: Memory bandwidth for reading the model’s weights
jd.m6.1.o3: The tokenizer’s rate of converting characters into ids
jd.m6.1.o4: The speed of transferring the weights from disk every step
jd.m6.2.q: In the course’s Llama example, what is stored in the KV cache?
jd.m6.2.e: Only keys and values. Queries, scores and MLP activations are computed and thrown away.
jd.m6.2.o1: Attention probabilities per layer and head
jd.m6.2.o3: Keys and values per position, layer and KV head
jd.m6.2.o4: Residual vectors before each MLP layer
jd.m6.3.q: Why is it correct to reuse K and V for old positions?
jd.m6.3.e: With fixed weights and the same prefix, a causal model’s earlier positions cannot depend on tokens appended later. Their K and V can therefore be reused; caching does not approximate them.
jd.m6.3.o1: Training makes the change in old keys and values negligible
jd.m6.3.o2: Causal attention keeps later tokens from changing old positions
jd.m6.3.o3: The sampler freezes old keys and values when choosing a token
jd.m6.3.o4: Position rotations correct changes in old keys and values

jd.m6.5.q: In the course’s idealized weight-bandwidth-bound decode example, the batch grows from 1 to 16 short-context sequences. What happens while compute and KV costs remain small?
jd.m6.5.e: One weight read serves many sequences, so the weight-transfer cost is shared. Real speedups depend on hardware, kernels, context and batch size; they stop scaling when other costs dominate.
jd.m6.5.o1: Step time grows about 16-fold; throughput stays similar
jd.m6.5.o2: Step time stays similar; throughput can approach 16-fold
jd.m6.5.o3: Step time drops about 16-fold; throughput grows even faster
jd.m6.5.o4: Step time stays similar; throughput also stays unchanged
jd.m6.6.q: What does TTFT mainly consist of?
jd.m6.6.e: The main server-side components are queueing and prefill. Tokenization, sampling, communication and other overhead can also contribute; TTFT is not the duration of the whole response.
jd.m6.6.o1: Queueing plus all decode steps of the completed response
jd.m6.6.o2: Queueing plus prompt prefill before the first token
jd.m6.6.o3: Model loading plus tokenization of the completed response
jd.m6.6.o4: The gaps between successive tokens after the first token
jd.m7.1.q: An MoE model has 100 B total parameters and 10 B active per token. With all weights resident on GPUs in bf16, how much aggregate memory do the weights alone need?
jd.m7.1.e: Resident weights use 100 B · 2 bytes ≈ 200 GB, before cache and other overhead. Active parameters describe work per token, not the total resident weight storage.
jd.m7.2.q: What decides which experts a token is sent to?
jd.m7.2.e: The router is trained together with the rest. Each layer has its own.
jd.m7.2.o1: A fixed table mapping each vocabulary id to a topic expert
jd.m7.2.o2: A learned router scoring the token vector at each layer
jd.m7.2.o3: A server scheduler assigning requests to the least busy experts
jd.m7.2.o4: A random draw independent of the token’s representation
jd.m7.3.q: Which of these gives the smallest KV cache per token and layer (d_h = 128)?
jd.m7.3.e: K and V together require 8,192 numbers for 32 heads, 2,048 for 8 heads, and 1,024 for 4 heads. The specified MLA representation uses 576 numbers.
jd.m7.3.o1: MHA: 32 KV heads, each with K and V of width 128
jd.m7.3.o2: GQA: 8 KV heads, each with K and V of width 128
jd.m7.3.o3: MLA: a cached representation of 576 numbers
jd.m7.3.o4: GQA: 4 KV heads, each with K and V of width 128
jd.m7.4.q: What does a long reasoning cost in an inference server?
jd.m7.4.e: Reasoning tokens are generated tokens: they consume decode time and KV memory. A longer reasoning trace can reduce how many concurrent sequences fit in the server.
jd.m7.4.o1: More prefill, with no extra decode
jd.m7.4.o2: More decode steps and a larger KV cache
jd.m7.4.o3: More weight memory, with unchanged KV
jd.m7.4.o4: More tokenization, with no extra compute
jd.m8.1.e: KV blocks are allocated as needed and need not be contiguous. With a block size of 16 tokens, each sequence wastes fewer than 16 token slots in its final partially filled block. This does not remove attention’s sequence-length cost.
jd.m8.1.o1: The quadratic number of query–key comparisons in full attention
jd.m8.1.o2: KV memory waste from large contiguous reservations
jd.m8.1.o3: The repeated loading of model weights from GPU memory
jd.m8.1.o4: The waiting time caused by sampling output tokens sequentially
jd.m8.2.q: What does a block table do?
jd.m8.2.e: The same idea as a page table in an operating system. The blocks do not have to sit next to each other.
jd.m8.2.o1: Maps sequence blocks to KV pool locations
jd.m8.2.o2: Maps waiting requests to batch slots
jd.m8.2.o3: Maps token ids to embedding table rows
jd.m8.2.o4: Maps transformer layers to GPU weight locations
jd.m8.3.q: For requests with the same model and cache configuration, what allows a prefix-cache hit in the course’s full-block example?
jd.m8.3.e: Each block’s hash builds on the previous block’s hash. A single deviating token early on breaks the chain from there.
jd.m8.3.o1: Same user, even with different starting tokens
jd.m8.3.o2: Same meaning, even with different token ids
jd.m8.3.o3: An identical token prefix covering cached full blocks
jd.m8.3.o4: Same sampling settings, even with different prompts
jd.m8.4.e: A slot that frees up is filled straight away by the next request in the queue.
jd.m8.4.o1: The active batch can change at every engine step

jd.m8.4.o3: All prompts are merged into one shared sequence

jd.m8.5.q: The startup log says: Maximum concurrency for 8,192 tokens per request: 47.50x. What does that mean?
jd.m8.5.e: The size of the KV pool in tokens divided by max-model-len. Shorter sequences mean more of them fit.
jd.m8.5.o1: Throughput is fixed at 47.5 requests per second

jd.m8.5.o3: Exactly 47 requests are launched in every batch

jd.m8.6.q: The preemption counter (vllm:num_preemptions_total in the reference example) keeps climbing. What is the likely cause?
jd.m8.6.e: Running requests exhaust the KV pool, so some are preempted and later recomputed. Reduce concurrent sequences or add KV capacity. Metric names depend on the installed vLLM version.
jd.m8.6.o1: The clients disconnect before their responses are finished
jd.m8.6.o2: The KV pool fills, forcing preemption and recomputation

jd.m8.7.q: Why does vLLM flatten the batch to [N_tokens, 4096]?
jd.m8.7.e: Matmuls do not care which request a row belongs to. Attention gets the boundaries via metadata.
jd.m8.7.o1: To let attention compare tokens belonging to unrelated requests
jd.m8.7.o2: To avoid padding requests with different token counts
jd.m8.7.o3: To reuse a single residual vector for every request in the batch

jd.m9.1.q: In the difference-of-means method, how is a candidate concept direction estimated in a layer’s residual stream?
jd.m9.1.e: Use mean(x | with) − mean(x | without) at comparable positions in a chosen layer. The result is a candidate direction, not proof that the concept has a unique or causal representation.

jd.m9.1.o2: Subtract mean activations without the concept from those with it

jd.final.11.o2: Each GPU holds shards of every layer and 4 KV heads
jd.final.11.o3: Each GPU has 16 complete layers and their KV heads
jd.final.11.o4: Each GPU has all weight matrices but only 4 KV heads
jd.final.12.q: What changes when the course’s residual-direction projection is baked into the weights?
jd.final.12.e: The output side of existing stream-writing matrices is projected away from the direction. The architecture and tensor shapes remain compatible with the same inference engine.
jd.final.12.o1: The number of blocks changes, but all weights stay unchanged
jd.final.12.o2: The residual width changes, requiring new attention matrix shapes
jd.final.12.o3: Stream-writing weight values change, but shapes stay unchanged
jd.final.12.o4: The vocabulary changes, requiring a new tokenizer and LM head
jd.gloss.1.def: An intermediate value computed during a forward pass. Changes for every token, unlike weights.
jd.gloss.2.def: An operation where several GPUs sum their partial results so that all of them end up with the same tensor. Used twice per layer with tensor parallelism.
jd.gloss.3.def: The part of the block where each position fetches information from earlier positions, weighted by how well its query matches a key.
jd.gloss.4.def: The model generates one token at a time, and every new token becomes input to the next step.
jd.gloss.5.def: Several sequences processed in the same forward pass.
jd.gloss.6.def: 16-bit floating point. The standard format for weights in inference: 2 bytes per parameter.
jd.gloss.7.def: A chunk of KV memory for a fixed number of tokens, 16 by default in vLLM.
jd.gloss.8.def: A per-sequence list that maps logical blocks to physical blocks in the KV pool.
jd.gloss.9.def: Byte Pair Encoding. A method for building a vocabulary by merging common character pairs.
jd.gloss.10.def: A rule in attention that makes position i see only positions 0..i.
jd.gloss.11.def: A template that turns a list of messages into a single string with special tokens.
jd.gloss.12.def: A long prompt is split over several steps so that it does not block other requests.
jd.gloss.13.def: Speed is limited by the GPU’s compute power. Applies to prefill.
jd.gloss.14.def: The composition of the batch is decided afresh at every step.
jd.gloss.15.def: A recorded chain of GPU calls that is replayed in one go to reduce CPU overhead.
jd.gloss.16.def: The width of the residual stream. 4096 in Llama-3-8B.
jd.gloss.17.def: The phase where tokens are generated one at a time using the KV cache.
jd.gloss.18.def: A table with one vector per token. The first step: id → vector.
jd.gloss.19.def: A transformer with a single stack, where each token sees the tokens before it. The GPT and Llama families are built this way.
jd.gloss.20.def: The original placement of normalization: the stream itself is normalized after every addition.
jd.gloss.21.def: An architecture from 2017 in which attention does most of the work. The foundation of today’s language models.
jd.gloss.22.def: One of several parallel MLPs in an MoE layer.
jd.gloss.23.def: Number of floating-point operations. Roughly 2 per parameter and token in a forward pass.
jd.gloss.24.def: 8-bit floating point. Halves memory compared with bf16.
jd.gloss.25.def: Grouped-Query Attention. Several query heads share one KV head, which shrinks the KV cache.
jd.gloss.26.def: Sampling that always picks the most probable token. Equivalent to temperature 0.
jd.gloss.27.def: One of several parallel attention computations in a layer. 32 query heads in Llama-3-8B.
jd.gloss.28.def: Inter-token latency, time per output token. The time between two tokens in the response.
jd.gloss.29.def: A vector that describes what a position offers. Compared with queries. Stored in the KV cache.
jd.gloss.30.def: Saved keys and values for all previous positions, per layer. Lets decode compute only the new position.
jd.gloss.31.def: Storing weights with fewer bits, for example FP8 or int4.
jd.gloss.32.def: One round of attention plus MLP, with 7 weight matrices and 2 norm weights. Llama-3-8B has 32.
jd.gloss.33.def: Passing the residual stream from an intermediate layer through the final norm and LM head, to see what the model “thinks” at that point.
jd.gloss.34.def: A file (often safetensors) that maps tensor names to weights, for example model.layers.5.self_attn.q_proj.weight.
jd.gloss.35.def: One of the 14,336 detectors in an MLP layer: a column in each of W_gate and W_up, and a row in W_down.
jd.gloss.36.def: A single weight matrix that transforms a vector, for example q_proj. Called a “linear layer” in PyTorch.
jd.gloss.37.def: A linear classifier trained on activations to see whether a feature is linearly represented.
jd.gloss.38.def: The last matrix, [d, V], that turns a vector into logits. Also called unembedding.
jd.gloss.39.def: One number per token in the vocabulary, before softmax.
jd.gloss.40.def: Speed is limited by how fast data can be read from memory. Applies to decode.
jd.gloss.41.def: Multi-head Latent Attention. K and V are compressed into a latent vector that is cached.
jd.gloss.42.def: The part of the block that processes each position on its own. Also called feed-forward.
jd.gloss.43.def: Mixture of Experts. The MLP is replaced by many experts, and a router picks a few per token.
jd.gloss.44.def: vLLM’s way of storing the KV cache in blocks with a block table, similar to virtual memory.
jd.gloss.45.def: The layers are split across GPUs: the first ones on one, the later ones on the next.
jd.gloss.46.def: A request is thrown out of the batch when KV memory runs out and is recomputed later.
jd.gloss.47.def: The phase where the whole prompt runs through the model at once and the KV cache is filled.
jd.gloss.48.def: KV blocks for a shared prompt prefix are reused across requests.
jd.gloss.49.def: Normalization before attention and the MLP instead of after.
jd.gloss.50.def: A vector that describes what a position is looking for. Computed and thrown away at every step.
jd.gloss.51.def: The per-position vector that runs through all layers and that every layer adds to.
jd.gloss.52.def: Normalization that scales a vector so that its RMS becomes 1.
jd.gloss.53.def: Rotary Position Embedding. Q and K are rotated depending on position.
jd.gloss.54.def: A small linear matrix in an MoE layer that scores each expert.
jd.gloss.55.def: The size of a tensor along each axis, for example [T, 4096].
jd.gloss.56.def: SiLU is a smooth variant of ReLU. SwiGLU is the MLP variant where SiLU(gate) is multiplied by up.
jd.gloss.57.def: Per token: which slot in the KV pool its K and V should be written to.
jd.gloss.58.def: Turns numbers into probabilities that sum to 1.
jd.gloss.59.def: A token with a special role, for example the start of the sequence or the end of a turn.
jd.gloss.60.def: A cheap guess at several tokens is verified by the large model in a single pass.
jd.gloss.61.def: Adding a direction to the residual stream to influence behavior.
jd.gloss.62.def: Sampling constrained by a grammar so that the output always follows a format.
jd.gloss.63.def: The number that logits are divided by before softmax. A low value gives a sharper distribution.
jd.gloss.64.def: Every weight matrix is split across several GPUs.
jd.gloss.65.def: Tokens per second, summed over all requests.
jd.gloss.66.def: A piece of text with an id in the vocabulary. Roughly a short word or part of a word.
jd.gloss.67.def: Cuts away unlikely tokens before sampling: the best k, or the smallest set that reaches probability p.
jd.gloss.68.def: Time to first token. Queue time plus prefill.
jd.gloss.69.def: The vector a position passes on when it is picked in attention. Stored in the KV cache.
jd.gloss.70.def: A learned number in the model. Fixed after training and used for every token.
jd.gloss.71.def: The set of all tokens. 128,256 in Llama 3.
